name: Arginine (AAKG)

chain: Bigger muscle pump, more blood flow
angle.text: Lifters take AAKG before training as a pre-workout 'pump' ingredient, hoping for fuller-looking muscles and better training output that adds up to more size over time. Small human trials have tested strength and performance rather than visible muscle size.

summary: Arginine alpha-ketoglutarate, a pre-workout 'pump' supplement whose small human trials mostly report no performance benefit.
note: Often sold inside stimulant-heavy pre-workouts; a case report links one such product to hemorrhagic stroke.
currentQuick:
AAKG is a salt of the amino acid L-arginine and alpha-ketoglutarate, marketed to lifters as a nitric oxide booster for muscle pumps, blood flow and endurance. It is a staple of pre-workout formulas.
Published human trials are few and small. Titles of several of them report that acute AAKG or arginine supplementation failed to improve muscular performance or endurance.
How it works: Arginine is the precursor of nitric oxide, which relaxes blood vessels. The marketing idea is that more arginine means more nitric oxide, more blood flow and a bigger pump. Alpha-ketoglutarate is a metabolic intermediate and glutamine precursor. Whether the combined salt raises nitric oxide better than plain arginine is not clearly established.
Risks and caveats: Grokipedia describes AAKG as generally tolerated at 3 to 6 g daily, with mild gastrointestinal upset at higher intakes. A 2012 case report described a hemorrhagic stroke in a young man after a multi-ingredient sports supplement (Jack3d) that contained other stimulants, so the cause cannot be attributed to AAKG alone.
deepLead:
Arginine alpha-ketoglutarate (AAKG) is a dietary supplement made of the amino acid L-arginine paired with alpha-ketoglutaric acid, typically in a 2:1 molar ratio, and marketed as more soluble or bioavailable than arginine alone. It is sold mainly to athletes and bodybuilders as a pre-workout ingredient intended to raise nitric oxide, improve muscle blood flow and increase strength or endurance.
Arginine is the sole precursor of nitric oxide in humans, a molecule that relaxes vascular smooth muscle. That physiology is the basis for the supplement's marketing, but controlled trials in trained and untrained men have generally not found a performance benefit from acute AAKG or arginine.

name: BCAA

angle.text: Lifters use BCAA powders around training to support muscle growth and cut soreness, so they can train more often and build a more muscular physique. The leucine mechanism is well described; trials of stand-alone BCAA supplements for muscle gain are limited.

summary: Leucine, isoleucine and valine powders sold for muscle and recovery; the mechanism is real but supplement-specific human evidence is limited.
note: Elevated blood BCAAs are associated with insulin resistance; long-term supplement effects are not settled.
currentQuick:
BCAAs are three essential amino acids found in dietary protein and sold separately as supplements for muscle gain and recovery. Leucine in particular triggers muscle protein-building pathways in lab studies.
Studies in people suggest possible reductions in muscle-damage markers and soreness, while effects on performance are described as neutral or unclear. Evidence specific to physique outcomes is limited.
How it works: Leucine activates the mTOR pathway that initiates muscle protein synthesis. BCAAs also act as metabolic signals affecting insulin signalling.
Risks and caveats: Sold as a dietary supplement. Higher circulating BCAAs are associated with obesity and insulin resistance, and some studies have raised questions about links with ALS in athletes and about lifespan in mice; these relationships are not fully established.
deepLead:
Branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs) are the three essential amino acids with a branched side chain: leucine, isoleucine and valine. Humans cannot synthesise them and obtain them from dietary protein . They are sold as stand-alone powders and capsules, mainly to people who lift weights, with claims about muscle growth, recovery and reduced soreness.
Leucine activates the mTOR signalling pathway involved in muscle protein synthesis, which is the main biological rationale for supplements; animal work shows leucine stimulates translation initiation in skeletal muscle . Human evidence for BCAA supplements specifically is more limited than the mechanistic work, and Wikipedia describes much of the exercise evidence as coming from small studies, animal models or reviews .
Separately, research has found that circulating BCAA levels are higher in people with obesity and insulin resistance, and animal studies have raised questions about long-term BCAA supplementation . In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities BCAAs are discussed as a muscle-building and recovery aid.

name: ZMA

chain: Zinc and magnesium for sleep and T
angle.text: Bodybuilders take ZMA at night in the hope of better sleep and higher testosterone, which they link to recovery and muscle gain. The few studies on those outcomes in trained athletes give conflicting results.

summary: A zinc, magnesium and B6 night-time supplement sold for sleep and testosterone; the few studies conflict.
note: Key supporting study was funded by the trademark holder.
currentQuick:
ZMA is a bundle of zinc, magnesium and vitamin B6, created by BALCO founder Victor Conte and sold to athletes as a pre-bed supplement.
A 1998 company-funded study reported strength gains, while later studies, including an industry-funded one, found no significant hormone or performance effects.
How it works: The claimed idea is that these minerals support sleep and anabolic hormone processes, with timing before bed intended to improve absorption.
Risks and caveats: Sold as a dietary supplement. Variants add 5-HTP, which can raise serotonin. Published safety data are not extensively covered in the available sources.
deepLead:
ZMA is a supplement combining zinc, magnesium and vitamin B6, marketed to athletes, gymnasts and bodybuilders. It was developed by Victor Conte, the founder of BALCO Laboratories . The standard formulation contains zinc monomethionine aspartate, magnesium aspartate and pyridoxine hydrochloride (vitamin B6) .
Its marketing centres on taking it before bed to support sleep and anabolic (muscle-building) processes. Published studies are few and conflict: a 1998 company-linked study reported strength gains in football players, while later studies found no effect on testosterone or performance . In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as a sleep and testosterone support supplement.

name: Beef organ / beef juice extract

angle.text: Beef organ and beef juice products are promoted as nutrient-dense support for muscle, so users can recover well and build a stronger physique. Evidence comes mainly from general nutrition knowledge about meat and offal; product-specific trials on muscle are thin.

summary: Concentrated beef organ or meat-juice products marketed as nutrient-dense muscle support; product-specific human evidence is thin.
note: No trials of branded organ or juice supplements for appearance outcomes were found.
currentQuick:
These are products made from beef organs or concentrated beef extract, sold as nutrient-dense supplements. Meat extract dates to Liebig in 1840.
Offal is a traditional food in many cuisines. Studies of organ or juice supplements for muscle are essentially absent; related work covers beef protein in general.
How it works: The idea is that concentrated meat protein and micronutrients support muscle and general health. A small registered study looked at hydrolysed beef absorption.
Risks and caveats: Sold as food or supplement. Older lab studies found mutagenic compounds forming in cooked beef and beef extract; relevance to modern products is not established.
deepLead:
Beef organ and beef juice or meat extract supplements are concentrated products derived from cattle meat or offal, sold as nutrient-dense foods or capsules for muscle and general health. Offal means the internal organs of a butchered animal, and these are eaten in many cuisines . Meat extract is a concentrated stock, first developed commercially in the nineteenth century .
No published trial reviewed here tests a branded organ or beef-juice capsule for muscle or appearance outcomes. A small registered study has examined the absorption and muscle-stimulating effect of hydrolysed minced beef . Evidence for the supplement category is therefore thin.

name: Dimethylglycine (DMG)

angle.text: DMG is sold for endurance, oxygen use and immune support, and users take it hoping for quicker recovery and more consistent training. Trials in other conditions have been small, and none examine appearance or training outcomes.

summary: A glycine derivative once called vitamin B16, sold for endurance and immunity; trials in other conditions have shown little benefit.
note: Athletic claims lack cited trial support.
currentQuick:
DMG is a natural metabolite of betaine and choline, found in beans and liver, and sold as a supplement for athletic endurance and immune support.
Trials in autism showed little difference from placebo, and a Cochrane review found no evidence in mitochondrial disease. No athletic trials are cited.
How it works: It sits in the methyl-donor pathway, produced from betaine and converted to sarcosine. It can act at the NMDA receptor glycine site in mice.
Risks and caveats: Labelled harmful if swallowed in concentrated form; rat oral LD50 is above 650 mg/kg. Human safety data are limited in the sources.
deepLead:
Dimethylglycine (DMG) is a derivative of the amino acid glycine with two methyl groups on the nitrogen. It forms during the breakdown of betaine (trimethylglycine) and choline, and occurs in foods such as beans and liver . It was once called vitamin B16, though it is not considered a true vitamin because deficiency causes no ill effects .
As a supplement it has been proposed as an athletic performance enhancer, immunostimulant, and treatment for autism, epilepsy and mitochondrial disease . Wikipedia reports that trials in autism spectrum disorders showed little to no difference from placebo and that a Cochrane review found no evidence of benefit in mitochondrial disease . Evidence for athletic or appearance outcomes is not provided in these sources. In looksmaxxing and recovery circles it is discussed as an endurance and oxygen-use aid.

name: Magnesium glycinate

angle.text: Magnesium glycinate is popular in looksmaxxing circles for sleep, relaxation and recovery, which users tie to a more rested face and better training. Sleep claims often rest on magnesium in general or on stacks with theanine and GABA, with few glycinate-specific trials.

summary: A glycine-bound magnesium supplement popular for sleep and calm; the claims outrun the glycinate-specific trials.
note: Severe kidney impairment is listed as a contraindication.
currentQuick:
Magnesium glycinate is magnesium bound to glycine, sold to address deficiency and popular for sleep and relaxation. It is about 14 percent elemental magnesium.
Marketing says it is gentler and better absorbed than oxide forms; glycinate-specific trials for sleep are few.
How it works: It supplies magnesium, a mineral involved in many enzyme and nerve functions, with glycine, which proponents say adds a calming effect.
Risks and caveats: Diarrhoea is the main reported effect, described as milder than with other forms. Severe renal impairment is listed as a contraindication in reference text.
deepLead:
Magnesium glycinate, also called magnesium bisglycinate or diglycinate, is the magnesium salt of glycine, containing about 14.1 percent elemental magnesium by mass . It is sold as a supplement to relieve magnesium deficiency and also appears in cosmetics . Marketing often presents it as better tolerated and more absorbable than magnesium oxide, and it is popular for sleep, relaxation and recovery .
Wikipedia does not address absorption, evidence or adverse effects . Human studies comparing magnesium compounds exist, but trials specifically on glycinate for sleep or appearance are limited in the sources reviewed here.

name: Magnesium malate

angle.text: Magnesium malate is promoted for energy, muscle soreness and recovery, so users can train more often in pursuit of a better physique. Direct human evidence for those uses is thin, with most claims coming from supplement sellers.

summary: Magnesium bound to malic acid, pitched for energy, soreness and fibromyalgia; direct human evidence is thin.
note: Bioavailability superiority claims rest on supplier sources.
currentQuick:
Magnesium malate pairs magnesium with malic acid and is sold to correct deficiency and for muscle soreness and recovery.
Claims of better absorption come from a supplier source; EFSA has evaluated it as a food ingredient.
How it works: It supplies magnesium, which is involved in muscle and nerve function; malate is an intermediate in energy metabolism, which sellers cite for energy claims.
Risks and caveats: Human safety data specific to this form are limited in the sources; EFSA assessed its use in foods and supplements.
deepLead:
Magnesium malate is the magnesium salt of malic acid, sold as a mineral supplement . Wikipedia notes it is discussed as more bioavailable than citrate or glycinate, citing a single supplier source . Supplement sellers also promote it for muscle soreness, exercise recovery and fibromyalgia pain .
The European Food Safety Authority has evaluated di-magnesium malate as a novel food ingredient and magnesium source . Human studies directly testing the malate form for appearance or performance are scarce in the sources reviewed.

name: Inositol nicotinate

angle.text: Inositol nicotinate is taken as a no-flush form of niacin, with users linking niacin to skin health and a healthier complexion. It has been studied for circulation in conditions such as intermittent claudication; nothing has been published on appearance.

summary: A no-flush niacin ester sold as a supplement; studied for circulation, with nothing published on appearance.
note: Evidence is limited to small circulation studies; liver effects are listed as for other niacin products.
currentQuick:
Inositol nicotinate is niacin bound to inositol, sold as a supplement that does not cause the usual niacin flush. It is included in appearance catalogues because of its niacin link.
Published research concerns circulation (Raynaud's phenomenon, leg pain on walking) and has produced mixed or unclear results. Nothing found examines skin or looks outcomes.
How it works: It is described as being broken down into inositol and niacin after ingestion; limited conversion to active niacin may explain the lack of flushing.
Risks and caveats: Generally described as safe orally, with stomach upset, gas, nausea and possible liver effects similar to other niacin products. Cautions are listed for diabetes, liver or kidney disease, bleeding disorders and gout. Sold over the counter in the US.
deepLead:
Inositol nicotinate, also called inositol hexanicotinate or inositol hexaniacinate, is a compound formed from niacin (vitamin B3) and inositol. In the United States it is sold as a dietary supplement, marketed as a "no-flush" form of niacin, and the body is described as breaking it down into its two components .
It has been studied mainly for circulation problems such as Raynaud's phenomenon and intermittent claudication rather than for skin or appearance. Wikipedia describes evidence for most other proposed uses, including cholesterol lowering, as unclear or insufficient . It is listed in appearance-oriented catalogues because of its relationship to niacin, but no published study found in the sources examines its effect on skin, hair or facial appearance.
Small thermographic studies from the late 1970s and early 1980s examined its effect on digital blood flow in Raynaud's phenomenon , and a UK health technology assessment evaluated it alongside other drugs for intermittent claudication .

name: Pyridoxamine

angle.text: Longevity and skin-focused users take pyridoxamine as an AGE inhibitor, on the theory that less glycation keeps collagen supple and slows visible skin ageing. It has been studied in diabetic kidney disease; no appearance research exists.

summary: A vitamin B6 form studied as an AGE inhibitor in diabetic kidney disease, with no appearance research.
note: The FDA ruled in 2009 it is not a legal dietary supplement in the US.
currentQuick:
Pyridoxamine is a natural form of vitamin B6 that is discussed as an inhibitor of advanced glycation end products, which are linked to tissue ageing and diabetic complications.
Its clinical development was for diabetic kidney disease and ended in 2016 when the sponsor ran out of funding. No study found tests it for skin or looks.
How it works: It is reported to trap reactive carbonyl intermediates, chelate metals and scavenge radicals, thereby limiting glycation and lipoxidation products.
Risks and caveats: Safety data are not detailed in the sources reviewed. In the US the FDA ruled in 2009 that pyridoxamine products are not dietary supplements under DSHEA.
deepLead:
Pyridoxamine is one of the three natural forms of vitamin B6. Its chemistry allows it to scavenge free radicals and reactive carbonyl compounds and to chelate metal ions . It is discussed in longevity and skin circles as an inhibitor of advanced glycation end products (AGEs), compounds linked in the literature to diabetic complications and tissue ageing .
Most research on it concerns diabetic kidney disease, where it was developed by Biostratum and later NephroGenex as the drug candidate Pyridorin . Animal studies reported protection of kidney and retina in diabetic rats . Its status in the United States is unusual: in 2009 the FDA ruled that pyridoxamine products fall outside the legal definition of a dietary supplement . No study found examines pyridoxamine for skin appearance.

name: D-Ribose-L-cysteine

angle.text: DRLC is marketed to raise glutathione, and users in longevity and skin circles hope for antioxidant protection that supports a healthier, younger look. Research is preclinical or on other conditions; nothing covers appearance.

summary: A patented cysteine prodrug marketed to raise glutathione; research is preclinical and nothing covers appearance.
note: Supporting claims come largely from developer-linked and animal or cell studies.
currentQuick:
D-Ribose-L-cysteine is a branded supplement ingredient designed to supply cysteine for glutathione, the body's main cellular antioxidant. It is mentioned in longevity contexts.
Published research is limited to cell and animal studies; no human trial was found and none addresses looks.
How it works: The ribose-cysteine ring is described as resisting oxidation until the cell releases cysteine, which the body uses to synthesise glutathione.
Risks and caveats: No human safety data were found in the sources reviewed. Claims of superiority over N-acetylcysteine rest on cell-culture and animal work described by a non-peer-reviewed reference.
deepLead:
D-Ribose-L-cysteine (DRLC), sold under the names RiboCeine and RibCys, is a patented synthetic compound intended to deliver L-cysteine to cells and so support the body's own glutathione production . Glutathione is a cellular antioxidant, and cysteine availability is described as the limiting factor in making it .
According to Grokipedia, an AI-generated reference, it was developed in the 1990s by Herbert T. Nagasawa at a Veterans Affairs medical center and the University of Minnesota, with patents assigned to Max International and the US Department of Veterans Affairs . It is catalogued in longevity circles rather than appearance communities. Published work found is preclinical; no human clinical study of it was found.

name: Eutropoflavin (7,8-DHF)

angle.text: 7,8-DHF is used by nootropic enthusiasts as a BDNF mimic for mood, cognition and recovery, with no direct appearance link drawn beyond general wellbeing. It has been studied in animals; no human studies exist.

summary: A plant flavone reported to activate the BDNF receptor TrkB in animals; no human studies exist.
note: Animal-only evidence; whether it directly activates TrkB has been questioned.
currentQuick:
7,8-DHF is a flavone reported in 2010 to mimic BDNF signalling at the TrkB receptor. It is discussed for brain and mood effects and appears in recovery-oriented lists.
All published work found is in cells and animals, with a low oral bioavailability in mice. No human trial was found.
How it works: It is described as binding TrkB and triggering signalling such as AKT, though a 2017 line of work questioned direct agonism.
Risks and caveats: No human safety data were found. Some in vitro effects, such as weak aromatase inhibition, have not been confirmed in living animals. It is not an approved drug.
deepLead:
7,8-Dihydroxyflavone (7,8-DHF), also called tropoflavin, is a naturally occurring flavone found in plants such as Godmania aesculifolia, Tridax procumbens and Primula vulgaris. It was reported in a 2010 PNAS paper as a small-molecule agonist of TrkB, the main receptor for brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) .
Sources differ on naming. Wikipedia uses the name eutropoflavin for the analogue 4'-dimethylamino-7,8-dihydroxyflavone , while Grokipedia applies it to that analogue as a synthetic compound reported from Emory University work . Supplement and forum use often applies the name to 7,8-DHF itself. Research is limited to cells and animals; no human clinical study was found.

name: 5-HTP (oxitriptan)

angle.text: In looksmaxxing circles 5-HTP is discussed as a serotonin precursor taken for mood and sleep, on the theory that better sleep shows up as clearer skin, less puffiness and a more rested face. Many trials cover mood and sleep; none address appearance.

summary: A serotonin precursor sold for mood and sleep; many trials registered, none about looks.
note: Serotonin syndrome has been reported with serotonin-elevating drugs; no FDA-approved 5-HTP drug.
currentQuick:
5-HTP is the step between tryptophan and serotonin and is sold as a supplement, often for sleep and mood.
Human trials exist across several conditions, but the sources reviewed do not report their outcomes, and none targets appearance.
How it works: It crosses the blood-brain barrier and is converted to serotonin; decarboxylase inhibitors such as carbidopa raise its effect.
Risks and caveats: Serotonin syndrome is a documented concern with serotonin-raising drugs. No FDA-approved medicine contains it as of 2025.
deepLead:
5-Hydroxytryptophan (5-HTP), medically oxitriptan, is a naturally occurring amino acid and intermediate in serotonin synthesis. The body makes it from tryptophan via tryptophan hydroxylase, the rate-limiting step, and unlike serotonin it crosses the blood-brain barrier . Food contains only insignificant amounts .
It is sold as a supplement for mood and sleep and is catalogued here as a sleep and recovery aid. Wikipedia states that, as of 2025, no FDA-approved medicines contain 5-HTP . Registered human trials have examined it for depression, mood, body composition, fatigue, satiety and sleep, though outcome data are not summarised in the sources used.

name: L-Tryptophan

angle.text: In looksmaxxing circles L-tryptophan is discussed as a serotonin and melatonin precursor taken for sleep and mood, on the theory that better sleep shows up as clearer skin, less puffiness and a more rested face. Sleep evidence is mixed, and appearance outcomes have not been studied.

summary: An essential amino acid sold for sleep and mood; evidence is weak and a 1989 contamination outbreak shaped its regulation.
note: Serotonin syndrome risk with SSRIs/MAOIs; 1989 EMS outbreak linked to contaminated batches.
currentQuick:
Tryptophan is an essential amino acid found in protein foods and the starting material for serotonin and melatonin. It is sold as a sleep and mood supplement.
Wikipedia cites a 2001 Cochrane review finding insufficient evidence and a 2017 sleep-medicine guideline advising against use for insomnia. No study found tests appearance outcomes.
How it works: Most is metabolised via the kynurenine pathway; a smaller share becomes serotonin and melatonin.
Risks and caveats: Side effects include nausea, drowsiness and headache; combining with SSRIs or MAOIs can cause serotonin syndrome. A 1989 outbreak of eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome, traced largely to contaminated batches, led to US restrictions lifted in 2001.
deepLead:
Tryptophan is an essential amino acid that humans cannot make and must obtain from protein foods such as meat, dairy, eggs, nuts and seeds. Besides building proteins it is a precursor of serotonin, melatonin and niacin . Frederick Hopkins first isolated it in 1901 from casein .
As a supplement it is marketed for sleep, mood and anxiety. Wikipedia reports the supporting evidence as weak: a 2001 Cochrane review found only two eligible studies with 64 participants and judged evidence insufficient, and the American Academy of Sleep Medicine's 2017 guideline advises against its use for insomnia . In 1989 supplements were linked to an outbreak of eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome (EMS) .

name: Ramelteon

angle.text: In looksmaxxing circles ramelteon is discussed as a prescription melatonin-receptor sleep aid for trouble falling asleep, on the theory that better sleep shows up as clearer skin, less puffiness and a more rested face. It is studied for insomnia in small medical trials; appearance has not been studied.

summary: A prescription melatonin-receptor sleep drug with small, medical-only evidence and nothing on appearance.
note: Prescription insomnia drug; no appearance studies exist.
currentQuick:
Ramelteon is a prescription drug for trouble falling asleep. It works on the same receptors as the body's own melatonin rather than on the GABA system.
Trials show it shortens the time to fall asleep by roughly 10 to 19 minutes versus placebo. No studies have examined it for appearance outcomes.
How it works: It activates MT1 and MT2 melatonin receptors thought to be involved in the sleep-wake rhythm, and is quickly cleared from the body.
Risks and caveats: Labelled adverse effects include somnolence, dizziness, fatigue and nausea, with rare allergic reactions and complex sleep behaviours. It is Rx-only in the US, not a controlled substance, and not authorised in the EU.
deepLead:
Ramelteon is a prescription melatonin receptor agonist taken by mouth for insomnia characterised by difficulty falling asleep. It binds the MT1 and MT2 melatonin receptors and, according to its US label, has no appreciable affinity for the GABA receptor complex used by benzodiazepines and Z-drugs . It was approved by the US FDA in 2005 under the brand name Rozerem and is not a controlled substance in the United States .
In the wiki's recovery category it is listed as a sleep-related compound. No published study has examined ramelteon for any appearance outcome, and no looksmaxxing community material about it was identified. Its documented use is medical.
Trials report small reductions in the time taken to fall asleep compared with placebo. The European Medicines Agency has not authorised it . The 2017 American Academy of Sleep Medicine guideline and later network meta-analyses place it among several insomnia drug options with modest effects .

name: Tasimelteon

angle.text: In looksmaxxing circles tasimelteon is discussed as a prescription circadian-rhythm drug used to align the sleep-wake cycle, on the theory that better sleep shows up as clearer skin, less puffiness and a more rested face. It is studied for non-24-hour disorder and Smith-Magenis sleep problems; appearance has not been studied.

summary: A prescription circadian drug approved for non-24-hour disorder in blind people; no appearance evidence.
note: Approved only for Non-24 and Smith-Magenis sleep disturbance.
currentQuick:
Tasimelteon is a melatonin-receptor drug approved in the US for Non-24-Hour Sleep-Wake Disorder, mainly seen in totally blind people, and for sleep problems in Smith-Magenis syndrome.
It is not an insomnia pill in general, and no research ties it to appearance.
How it works: It activates MT1 and MT2 melatonin receptors involved in circadian timing; the label says exactly how it works in Non-24 is unclear.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects include headache, raised liver enzyme ALT, vivid dreams or nightmares and infections. The label warns of somnolence. It is prescription-only.
deepLead:
Tasimelteon is a prescription melatonin MT1/MT2 receptor agonist developed by Vanda Pharmaceuticals and sold as Hetlioz. The US FDA approved it in January 2014 for Non-24-Hour Sleep-Wake Disorder in adults, and in December 2020 for nighttime sleep disturbances in Smith-Magenis syndrome .
Non-24 is a circadian rhythm disorder mainly affecting totally blind people. Tasimelteon is not a general insomnia or appearance product. No published study has examined it for appearance, and no looksmaxxing community material about it was found.
Phase 3 trials in totally blind people (SET and RESET) reported entrainment of the circadian rhythm in a minority of patients on treatment .

name: Agomelatine

angle.text: Agomelatine is a melatonin-linked antidepressant that some users consider for sleep and mood, on the theory that better sleep and lower stress show up in the face. It is studied for depression; appearance has not been studied.

summary: A melatonin-linked antidepressant sold in Europe, not the US; no appearance evidence.
note: Liver enzyme monitoring is part of prescribing; not FDA approved.
currentQuick:
Agomelatine is a prescription antidepressant authorised in the EU and some other countries but not in the US. It acts on melatonin receptors as well as a serotonin receptor.
No studies tie it to appearance, and it appears here because of its sleep and circadian angle.
How it works: It activates MT1 and MT2 melatonin receptors and blocks 5-HT2C receptors, which preclinical work links to increased dopamine and noradrenaline in the frontal cortex.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects include headache, nausea, dizziness and sleepiness. Raised liver enzymes have been reported, so liver testing is part of use, and it is contraindicated in hepatic impairment.
deepLead:
Agomelatine is an antidepressant developed by Servier and sold as Valdoxan. It is an agonist at melatonin MT1 and MT2 receptors and an antagonist at serotonin 5-HT2C receptors . It was authorised in the European Union in 2009 and is available in several other countries, but it has not been approved by the US FDA .
It is listed in the wiki's recovery category because of its sleep-related, melatonin-linked mechanism. No study has examined it for appearance, and no looksmaxxing community discussion of it was identified.
Network meta-analysis of antidepressants has compared it with other agents for major depression . Liver monitoring is part of its use because of reports of raised liver enzymes .

name: Hydroxyzine

angle.text: In looksmaxxing circles hydroxyzine is discussed as a sedating antihistamine used for anxiety, itch and sleep, on the theory that better sleep shows up as clearer skin, less puffiness and a more rested face. It is studied for anxiety and itch; its effect on looks has not been studied.

summary: A sedating prescription antihistamine for anxiety and itch; nothing on appearance.
note: Sedating; additive with alcohol and other depressants.
currentQuick:
Hydroxyzine is an older prescription antihistamine used for anxiety, allergic itching and sedation around surgery.
No research links it to appearance outcomes; it is listed because of its sleep-aiding and anti-itch uses.
How it works: It blocks histamine H1 receptors and, because it enters the brain, causes sedation.
Risks and caveats: Drowsiness, dry mouth and dizziness are common. Labels warn about combined sedation with alcohol, rare heart rhythm effects and seizures, and use in early pregnancy.
deepLead:
Hydroxyzine is a first-generation antihistamine of the piperazine class, approved by the US FDA in 1956. Its US label covers symptomatic relief of anxiety and tension, itching from allergic conditions such as chronic urticaria and atopic or contact dermatitis, and sedation before and after general anaesthesia .
It appears in the wiki's recovery category because of its sedative and anti-itch uses. No studies were found on hydroxyzine for appearance outcomes, and no looksmaxxing community discussion was identified.
Reviews list it among treatments for anxiety disorders and for urticaria . Its sedating effect is linked to its ability to cross into the brain .

name: Low-dose doxepin (Silenor)

angle.text: In looksmaxxing circles low-dose doxepin is discussed as a prescription option for staying asleep through the night, on the theory that better sleep shows up as clearer skin, less puffiness and a more rested face. It is studied for sleep-maintenance insomnia; appearance has not been studied.

summary: A prescription low-dose tricyclic approved for sleep-maintenance insomnia; no appearance evidence.
note: Anticholinergic and sedating; Rx-only.
currentQuick:
Low-dose doxepin (Silenor) is a prescription sleep medicine approved in 2010 for staying asleep. It is a tricyclic antidepressant sold at much lower strengths for this purpose.
No studies link it to appearance outcomes.
How it works: At low strengths it mainly blocks histamine H1 receptors, producing sedation; at antidepressant strengths reuptake inhibition predominates.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects include sedation, dry mouth, constipation and blood pressure drops on standing. It is contraindicated with MAO inhibitors and is Rx-only.
deepLead:
Doxepin is a tricyclic compound first approved by the US FDA in 1969 as an antidepressant under the brand name Sinequan. A low-dose oral tablet, Silenor, was approved in 2010 for insomnia characterised by difficulty staying asleep . A 5% topical cream is approved for itching in atopic dermatitis or lichen simplex chronicus .
At the low strengths sold for insomnia, doxepin's sedating effect is attributed mainly to histamine H1 receptor antagonism . No study has examined it for appearance outcomes, and no looksmaxxing community material was identified.
The American Academy of Sleep Medicine 2017 guideline includes low-dose doxepin among its recommendations for sleep maintenance insomnia .

name: Suvorexant

angle.text: In looksmaxxing circles suvorexant is discussed as an orexin-blocking prescription sleep drug, on the theory that better sleep shows up as clearer skin, less puffiness and a more rested face. Insomnia data are solid; appearance has not been studied.

summary: A prescription orexin-blocking sleep drug; solid insomnia data, no appearance evidence.
note: Schedule IV controlled substance in the US.
currentQuick:
Suvorexant (Belsomra) is a prescription insomnia drug approved in 2014 that blocks the brain's wake-promoting orexin signals.
Trials support effects on falling and staying asleep; no studies link it to appearance outcomes.
How it works: It competitively blocks orexin A and B at OX1 and OX2 receptors, reducing arousal rather than broadly depressing the central nervous system through GABA.
Risks and caveats: Next-day somnolence, headache and dizziness are reported, with rare complex sleep behaviours. It is Schedule IV in the US and interacts with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors and alcohol.
deepLead:
Suvorexant is a dual orexin receptor antagonist developed by Merck and sold as Belsomra. The US FDA approved it in August 2014 as the first drug of its class for insomnia characterised by difficulty with sleep onset and/or maintenance . It blocks orexin A and B at OX1 and OX2 receptors, reducing wake-promoting signalling rather than acting through GABA .
It is Schedule IV in the US . No study has examined it for appearance, and no looksmaxxing community discussion was identified.

deepLead:
Lemborexant, sold as Dayvigo, is a prescription oral medicine for adults with insomnia involving trouble falling asleep, staying asleep, or both. It was developed by Eisai and belongs to the dual orexin receptor antagonist (DORA) class, which blocks the wake-promoting orexin (hypocretin) signalling system rather than enhancing GABA activity as benzodiazepines and Z-drugs do.
The US Food and Drug Administration approved it in December 2019, and it is a Schedule IV controlled substance in the United States. Phase 3 trials have compared it with placebo and with zolpidem extended-release in older adults, and a 12-month trial has reported longer-term efficacy and tolerability data.
Lemborexant has no approved cosmetic or appearance indication, and no published study has tested it for appearance outcomes. Its relevance to looksmaxxing discussions is indirect, through the wider topic of sleep quality and recovery. Reported adverse effects include somnolence, headache, and abnormal dreams, and its label carries warnings about next-day impairment and complex sleep behaviors.
